offtopic: I finally tried roasting the broccoli before adding it to pasta. Took an extra tray, but the crispy edges made washing up worth it.
My bus arrived early for once and I still missed it. Apparently leaving the house at my usual time was the wrong strategy today.
I started a little herb garden on the windowsill. The basil looks great and the parsley looks like it wants to move out.
That cooking show has become my laundry background noise. I keep missing the actual recipes while matching socks.
I bought a quieter keyboard this week. It feels strange, but I can finally type late without hearing every key across the room.
Made it through the first boss after several terrible attempts. Taking a break apparently helped more than all my equipment upgrades.

items.post_a: I count just one thing on the sculptor’s table. Calling it clay or calling it a statue gives me different descriptions of that very same object.
items.post_b: I still count one object, though the statue label only fits while it has the relevant shape. Squashing it changes what I can call it without adding or removing a second occupant.
fillers: If I weigh the clay statue, I am weighing the clay itself. I do not think there are two objects there just because I can describe its material and its shape.
The gallery label makes the clay sound grander, but I see the statue as that lump shaped a certain way. Giving it a title does not multiply what is on display.
items.note: B limits when the statue description applies while preserving the claim that there is one object.

items.post_a: I think caring for someone can give a life real meaning even when the caregiver feels completely numb about it. Their enthusiasm is not what makes that work matter.
items.post_b: I would not say every useful chore makes a life meaningful. Sustained care for another person seems like a better example of something that matters even when the person doing it feels detached.
fillers: When I read about someone quietly keeping a relative safe for years, I see meaning in that life. It does not disappear because they never found the experience personally fulfilling.
I do not think a person has to recognize the worth of their own contribution for it to count. Helping someone recover can matter beyond whatever satisfaction the helper gets.
items.note: B narrows which activities qualify without making meaning depend entirely on personal attitudes.

items.post_a: I would call the Mars arrival me. If the machine carries over my memories, personality, and whole mental life exactly, destroying the old body does not end my survival.
items.post_b: A forum commenter argued that the scanner amounts to an execution, with a fresh copy waking up on Mars afterward. I understand their story, but I am reporting their position here, not endorsing it.
fillers: I would use the transporter to visit Mars without thinking I was sacrificing myself. What matters to me is that my mental life picks up there exactly where it left off.
The replacement body does not bother me in that example. I regard the person remembering my departure on Mars as my continued existence, rather than merely a convincing souvenir.
items.note: B attributes the death-and-copy account to another commenter and explicitly declines to adopt it.

items.post_a: I think believing something means standing in a particular relationship to a representation inside your mind. Wanting something involves that internal setup too, just with a different attitude toward it.
items.post_b: For me, a desire involves mentally representing how things could be and wanting that scenario realized. A belief involves taking a represented situation to describe how things actually are.
fillers: I can believe the shop is closed while sitting completely still. The belief is my accepting an internal representation of the shop as closed, whether or not I do anything about it.
When I want a holiday, I have some version of that holiday represented mentally and an attitude toward it. That is what I take the desire itself to consist in.
items.note: B repeats the account of beliefs and desires as attitudes toward internal representations.

items.post_a: I judge whether a belief is justified entirely by what its holder can reach through reflection. Hidden facts about how their mind works cannot supply an extra reason they cannot access.
items.post_b: A dependable perceptual process can confer warrant even when its user has no insight into its workings. I consider that unseen track record enough to make accepting its output reasonable.
fillers: If two people have exactly the same reasons available when they look inward, I give their beliefs the same justification. Information neither can reflectively access should not change that assessment.
I would ask someone to examine their evidence and how it supports their conclusion. As I see it, that accessible material fully settles whether they are justified in believing it.
items.note: B endorses warrant from inaccessible reliability using different vocabulary and no announcement of change.

offtopic: I tried making pancakes in my smallest pan and spent most of breakfast waiting. Next time I am using the big one immediately.
My headphones got tangled inside a zipped pocket somehow. I put them away neatly, so I would really like an explanation from the pocket.
I finished the season last night. The ending felt rushed, but the middle episodes were good enough that I will probably watch another.
Went for a walk after the rain and came back with soaked shoes. The shortcut through the grass was less clever than it looked.
I reorganized my game inventory instead of doing the next mission. At least I can finally find the healing items now.
The new grocery layout has completely defeated me. I found rice twice before finding the bread I actually went in for.

items.post_a: I think natural selection primarily sorts whole living creatures. Their combined traits determine how they fare and reproduce, so the organism is where I place the main unit of selection.
items.post_b: I think natural kinds reflect real divisions in the world. Calling two samples gold tracks something they share independently of whatever filing system we happen to prefer.
fillers: A rabbit survives with its whole collection of traits working together. That is why I treat the complete animal as the primary thing natural selection acts on.
Watching birds compete for food makes the organism level feel basic to me. I see natural selection chiefly filtering integrated creatures through their success at staying alive and reproducing.
items.d5_other_question: Are natural kinds real divisions in the world or merely human classifications?
items.note: B concerns whether natural kinds are mind-independent, not which entities natural selection primarily acts on.

items.post_a: I think my deepest reasons to act come from what helps a human life go well. Friendship and developing my abilities can give me reasons even before I feel like pursuing them.
items.post_b: The essay I read grounds every reason for acting in some desire the agent already has. I can explain that view for the discussion, but it is the author’s account, not mine.
fillers: I can have a reason to repair a friendship even when I would rather avoid the awkward conversation. To me, the source is its place in a flourishing life.
Sometimes I need to develop better wants instead of following my current ones. I think the reasons for doing that come from what actually helps me live well as a person.
items.note: B reports an author’s desire-based account without adopting it.

items.post_a: I see one object when I look at a clay statue. The lump and the sculpture are the same thing, described with attention to different features.
items.post_b: Giving the shaped clay a spot in a gallery does not put another object on its pedestal. I count the statue as that very piece of clay.
fillers: I would list one object if someone asked me to inventory that clay sculpture. Mentioning what it is made from does not give me another thing to list.
When I pick up the statue, I pick up the lump itself. I do not think the artistic description names something additional sitting in the same space.
items.note: B restates that statue and clay are one object.

items.post_a: I think a life gets all its meaning from the commitments and interests of the person living it. Nothing becomes meaningful for me independently of what I care about or choose.
items.post_b: If caring for strangers gave a life meaning independently of anyone’s commitments, then even an unwilling helper could have a meaningful life through that work. I am exploring that premise, not saying I accept it.
fillers: I do not see a universal list of projects that automatically makes a life meaningful. For me, meaning comes entirely from the person investing their care or choices in something.
My little projects matter because I make them part of what I care about. I think that personal attachment or choice is the whole source of meaning, however impressive the project looks.
items.note: B explores what follows from objective meaning under an explicit unendorsed assumption.

items.post_a: I think some arrangements genuinely make a larger object and others do not. A working bicycle qualifies for me; a loose collection of unrelated things does not automatically become one more thing.
items.post_b: The book’s author says any collection counts as a further object, even my shoe together with a distant satellite. That is their extremely permissive account; I am describing it without signing on.
fillers: I count the assembled chair as an object, but I do not count every scattered handful of its parts as another one. Composition seems to require something that arbitrary collections lack.
I cannot get behind treating every random grouping as a thing of its own. Some pieces really form a larger whole, while other collections remain just several things.
items.note: B attributes unrestricted composition to a book’s author and does not endorse it.

offtopic: I baked potatoes and forgot to poke holes in them. Nothing exploded, but I spent the entire cooking time watching the oven suspiciously.
The train was quiet enough this morning that I actually finished a chapter. Usually I just reread the same paragraph between announcements.
I moved my desk closer to the window. The afternoon glare is annoying, but having some daylight while I work feels worth it.
Finally beat that puzzle level after realizing the blue switch could be pressed twice. I had invented a much harder game in my head.
I watched the first episode while eating dinner and immediately started the second. So much for getting to bed early tonight.
My grocery delivery substituted tiny apples for the big ones. They are good, but eating three feels like an unnecessarily elaborate snack.

items.post_a: I put whole organisms at the center of natural selection. An animal succeeds or fails as an integrated creature, so that is the primary unit getting selected.
items.post_b: I think genes are the basic units of natural selection. Their persistence through successive bodies is the central story, while organisms are the temporary arrangements carrying them along.
fillers: A bird’s traits have to work together in an actual bird. I take that complete living package to be the primary target of natural selection.
When I think about which creatures leave offspring, I see selection mainly operating on organisms. The entire animal has to survive and reproduce in its environment.
items.note: B plainly replaces organisms with genes as the fundamental units of selection.

items.post_a: I think numbers exist even though they are not anywhere and never began at any moment. Abstract things are part of reality without needing an address in space or time.
items.post_b: I am less confident now that numbers exist independently of everything physical. The demand to explain what their existence amounts to bothers me, but I have not settled on denying abstract things.
fillers: The number seven does not seem like something people created by writing a symbol. I think it exists independently, outside the places and dates where we use it.
I cannot picture a set floating somewhere, but I do not think that counts against it. I regard sets as real abstract things that have no location or lifespan.
items.note: B expresses uncertainty about abstract existence without asserting that only concrete things exist.

items.post_a: I would take both boxes in Newcomb’s problem. Whatever the predictor already put inside, grabbing the clear one adds a thousand dollars, so I see that as the rational choice.
items.post_b: My recommendation is to leave the visible cash untouched and collect the concealed payout alone. With such an accurate forecaster, passing up that tempting extra grand is the sensible strategy.
fillers: I cannot affect the earlier prediction when I stand in front of the boxes. I would collect both, because that gives me an extra thousand regardless of the hidden contents.
Even with the impressive prediction record, I would choose both boxes. For either amount already sitting in the opaque one, taking the clear one too increases my winnings.
items.note: B recommends only the concealed payout using different wording, without acknowledging a change.

items.post_a: I think the continuum hypothesis has a definite answer, even if our usual axioms cannot settle it. There is a fact about those infinite sizes for us to discover.
items.post_b: I think the physical continuum is an idealization rather than the literal structure of space. Smooth geometry can describe measurements well without space actually containing endlessly divisible distances.
fillers: The limits of a proof system do not persuade me that the continuum hypothesis is unsettled in reality. I think it is either true or false independently of what we can prove.
I distinguish our inability to decide the continuum hypothesis from its having no answer. For me, there is a determinate mathematical fact even if our tools never reach it.
items.d5_other_question: Is the physical continuum a literal feature of space or a mathematical idealization?
items.note: B discusses whether physical space is a continuum, not the truth value of the continuum hypothesis.

items.post_a: I think every fact has an explanation, including facts we will never manage to explain ourselves. Running out of answers does not mean reality has run out of reasons.
items.post_b: I am starting to wonder whether demanding an explanation for absolutely everything goes too far. The idea of a stopping point has some pull, but I have not concluded that any fact is inexplicable.
fillers: When an explanation ends with something unexplained, I assume there is more to understand. I do not think any fact simply lacks an explanation altogether.
I see the universe’s existence as another fact calling for an explanation. Not knowing that explanation does not make me think there is none.
items.note: B questions universal explanation without committing to any brute facts.

offtopic: I made soup with whatever vegetables were left in the fridge. It came out better than the meal I actually planned earlier this week.
My usual walking route is blocked by construction again. The detour adds ten minutes, which would be nicer if it passed a bakery.
I started a new farming save and immediately planted more crops than I could water. Apparently I learned nothing from the last one.
The show I am watching keeps ending episodes halfway through a conversation. It works on me every time, which is getting annoying.
I washed my backpack and found a receipt from ages ago in a pocket. The bag is clean now; the receipt did not survive.
Tried cold noodles for lunch because it was too warm to cook much. I went overboard on the sauce, but I would make them again.

items.post_a: I think if I sincerely believe I ought to do something, I must have at least a tiny push toward doing it. I can resist that push, but it cannot be completely absent.
items.post_b: I am less sure that a sincere moral judgment always supplies even a little motivation. Some accounts of total indifference are troubling, though I have not decided those cases really separate the two.
fillers: I can know I ought to apologize and still avoid it all week. I think the genuine judgment supplies some motivation, even when embarrassment easily overwhelms it.
To me, sincerely judging that I should help includes some pull toward helping. That pull might be weak enough to lose against nearly everything else I want.
items.note: B doubts the necessary connection without asserting that sincere judgment can occur with zero motivation.

items.post_a: I think doing the right thing comes down to respecting people’s rights and meeting our duties. A better total outcome does not make violating those basic constraints morally right.
items.post_b: I am trying out a challenge: why should I keep a duty if breaking it produces the best overall result? Could maximizing the consequences be the whole basis of right action?
fillers: I would not call framing an innocent person right just because it calms a crowd. I see respecting their rights as the basic moral requirement, regardless of the payoff.
When I assess an action, I put duties and rights first. I do not think favorable consequences can turn a violation of those requirements into the right act.
items.note: B explicitly poses a challenge and asks about consequentialism without endorsing it.

items.post_a: I think some facts simply have no explanation. At some point reality just is a certain way, and asking why does not guarantee there is an answer waiting.
items.post_b: I am wondering how someone could defend the claim that absolutely every fact has an explanation. Would that require an endless chain, or could a final explanation account for itself too?
fillers: I do not assume the existence of the universe has a further reason behind it. I think reality includes brute facts, even if identifying a particular one is difficult.
An endless demand for reasons does not convince me that reasons are always available. My view is that some facts really are inexplicable, rather than merely unexplained so far.
items.note: B asks how universal explanation could work without adopting it.

items.post_a: I think genes are the fundamental things natural selection sorts. Bodies come and go, but the copying and persistence of genetic variants is the basic process I am tracking.
items.post_b: I used to put genes at the center, but I have changed my mind. I now think whole organisms are the primary units of natural selection, since their integrated lives determine survival and reproduction.
fillers: Following a gene through generations makes more sense to me than treating each body as the basic unit. I see organisms as carriers in a selection process fundamentally centered on genes.
The variants that keep getting copied are what I take natural selection to be fundamentally about. For me, genes remain the basic units even when their effects involve an entire animal.
items.note: B explicitly announces a change from gene-centered to organism-centered selection.

items.post_a: I think numbers and sets really exist apart from the physical world. They do not occupy a place or happen at a time, but that does not make them imaginary.
items.post_b: I think everything real exists somewhere in space and time. Numbers and sets are ways we describe concrete things, not additional abstract entities existing outside the physical world.
fillers: I do not think numbers depend on anyone having counted something. In my view they exist timelessly, with no location, whether or not a mind ever considers them.
I see mathematics as investigating real abstract objects. A set does not need to sit anywhere or last for a stretch of time to exist.
items.note: B plainly denies abstract entities and asserts that everything existing is concrete and spatiotemporal.
